title: Relative clauses and housing
objectives: I can describe people, places and things with a relative clause that opens with 'яки́й', taking its gender and number from the noun it describes and its case from its job in the clause.
I can use 'що' as a relative word, and 'той, хто', 'усі́, хто' and 'те, що' for 'whoever', 'everyone who' and 'what'.
I can say where, where to, where from and whose in a relative clause with 'де', 'куди́', 'зві́дки' and 'чий', and set off every relative clause with commas.
I can read apartment advertisements, ask a landlord about an apartment and say where furniture stands or lies.
I can explain the spelling and sound of 'две́рі', 'на по́версі' and 'оголо́шення'.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'буди́нку', with a fleeting 'о'. It names any building, most often an apartment building in a city. 'Ха́та' is a traditional village house, and 'дім' is a house or a home.

example.target: Буди́нок, яки́й стої́ть бі́ля па́рку, нови́й.
example.source: The building that stands by the park is new.
example.source_literal: Building, which stands near park, new.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'по́верху'; locative 'на по́версі', always with 'на'. It is a level of a building. The floor at street level is 'пе́рший по́верх'.

example.source: I live on the third floor.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'лі́фта'. You go up 'на лі́фті', by elevator, with 'на' as for other means of transport.

example.target: У буди́нку, де живе́ Окса́на, нема́є лі́фта.
example.source: There is no elevator in the building where Oksana lives.
example.source_literal: In building, where lives Oksana, there-is-not of-elevator.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'балко́на'; locative 'на балко́ні'. You step out 'на балко́н', with the accusative of direction.

example.target: Зі спа́льні мо́жна ви́йти на балко́н.
example.source: You can step out onto the balcony from the bedroom.
example.source_literal: From bedroom possible to-go-out onto balcony.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'спа́ти', to sleep: the room for sleeping. Genitive and locative 'спа́льні'.

example.source: The bed is in the bedroom.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'віта́ти', to greet or welcome: the room where a family receives its guests. Genitive and locative 'віта́льні'.

example.target: Дива́н стої́ть у віта́льні, бі́ля вікна́.
example.source: The sofa is in the living room, by the window.
example.source_literal: Sofa stands in living-room, near window.

vocabulary.note: It has no singular form, so it names one door or several, and the words that agree with it are plural. Genitive 'двере́й', with the stress on the ending.
It has no singular form and names furniture as a whole, so its adjectives and verbs are plural: 'нові́ ме́блі'. Genitive 'ме́блів'.

example.target: Усі́ ме́блі, які́ тут стоя́ть, нові́.
example.source: All the furniture here is new.
example.source_literal: All furniture, which here stand, new.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'лі́жка'; locative 'на лі́жку'. Ukrainian usually says 'спа́ти на лі́жку', literally to sleep on the bed, where English says in bed; 'у лі́жку' is also correct.

example.target: Я сплю на лі́жку, яке́ мені́ дала́ бабу́ся.
example.source: I sleep in a bed that my grandmother gave me.
example.source_literal: I sleep on bed, which to-me gave grandma.

vocabulary.note: A tall piece of furniture with doors, for clothes, books or dishes. Locative 'у ша́фі'.

example.target: Ша́фа, яку́ ми купи́ли, не ду́же вели́ка.
example.source: The wardrobe we bought is not very big.
example.source_literal: Wardrobe, which we bought, not very big.

example.target: Дива́н, на яко́му сиди́ть Тара́с, ду́же зру́чний.
example.source: The sofa Taras is sitting on is very comfortable.
example.source_literal: Sofa, on which sits Taras, very comfortable.

vocabulary.note: 'Оренду́ю', 'оренду́єш', 'оренду́ють', like 'працюва́ти'. It has no aspect partner: the one verb serves as both, and the context decides. It names what the tenant does, and the person rented from follows 'у' or 'в' with the genitive: 'Я оренду́ю кварти́ру в Богда́на.'
Genitive 'вла́сника'. A woman who owns something is 'вла́сниця'. Both are built from the adjective 'вла́сний', own.

example.target: Вла́сник, з яки́м я говори́в, живе́ у Льво́ві.
example.source: The landlord I talked to lives in Lviv.
example.source_literal: Owner, with whom I talked, lives in Lviv.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'оголоси́ти', to announce. The genitive singular and the nominative plural are also 'оголо́шення'. It covers an ad for an apartment or a job and a notice on a wall.

example.target: Я прочита́в оголо́шення, яке́ ви написа́ли.
example.source: I read the advertisement you wrote.
example.source_literal: I read advertisement, which you wrote.

vocabulary.note: It describes furniture that is comfortable ('зру́чний дива́н') and a place or a time that suits you ('зру́чний час').

example.source: The apartment is convenient because the metro is close.

vocabulary.note: It describes a room with a lot of daylight, and also a light color. It is stressed on the ending in every form: 'світла́', 'світле́', 'світлі́'.
The predicative word built from it is 'ти́хо', like 'те́пло' from 'те́плий': 'Тут ти́хо.', it is quiet here, literally 'here quiet'.

example.target: Це ти́хий буди́нок, де живу́ть сі́м’ї з дітьми́.
example.source: This is a quiet building where families with children live.
example.source_literal: This quiet building, where live families with children.

vocabulary.note: Built from 'га́лас', noise or din. It describes people, streets and places.

example.target: Сусі́ди, які́ живу́ть над на́ми, ду́же галасли́ві.
example.source: The neighbors who live above us are very noisy.
example.source_literal: Neighbors, which live above us, very noisy.

vocabulary.note: 'Лежу́', 'лежи́ш', 'лежа́ть', like 'сиді́ти'. Ukrainian often says where a thing is with a verb of position: 'стоя́ти' for something upright, such as a wardrobe, a table or books on a shelf, and 'лежа́ти' for something lying flat, such as a key or a book on a table. The perfective 'полежа́ти' means to lie for a while.

example.target: Кни́га, що лежи́ть на столі́, моя́.
example.source: The book on the table is mine.
example.source_literal: Book, that lies on table, mine.

dialogues.title: Calling about an advertisement
dialogues.context: Sam is looking for an apartment and phones Bohdan, who owns an apartment that Sam read about in an advertisement. They have never met, so they say 'ви'.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́брий день! Мене́ зва́ти Сем. Я дзвоню́ про оголо́шення, яке́ я прочита́в сього́дні вра́нці.
lines.source: Hello! My name is Sam. I'm calling about the advertisement I read this morning.
lines.source_literal: Good day! Me to-call Sam. I phone about advertisement, which I read today in-the-morning.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́брий день. Про яку́ кварти́ру ви пита́єте? У ме́не їх дві.
lines.source: Hello. Which apartment are you asking about? I have two.
lines.source_literal: Good day. About which apartment you ask? At me of-them two.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Про ту, що ма́є балко́н.
lines.source: The one with a balcony.
lines.source_literal: About that, that has balcony.

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Так, звича́йно. Ця кварти́ра ще ві́льна. Вона́ на тре́тьому по́версі, і в буди́нку є ліфт.
lines.source: Yes, of course. That apartment is still available. It's on the third floor, and the building has an elevator.
lines.source_literal: Yes, of-course. This apartment still free. It on third floor, and in building there-is elevator.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре. А скі́льки там кімна́т?
lines.source: Good. And how many rooms does it have?
lines.source_literal: Good. And how-many there of-rooms?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Дві. Віта́льня й спа́льня, з яко́ї мо́жна ви́йти на балко́н. Ще є ку́хня й ва́нна.
lines.source: Two. A living room and a bedroom that opens onto the balcony. There's also a kitchen and a bathroom.
lines.source_literal: Two. Living-room and bedroom, from which possible to-go-out onto balcony. Also there-is kitchen and bathroom.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А ме́блі в кварти́рі є?
lines.source: And is there furniture in the apartment?
lines.source_literal: And furniture in apartment there-is?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Так. Є лі́жко, ша́фа, дива́н і стіл, яки́й стої́ть на ку́хні.
lines.source: Yes. There's a bed, a wardrobe, a sofa and a table, which is in the kitchen.
lines.source_literal: Yes. There-is bed, wardrobe, sofa and table, which stands on kitchen.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А сусі́ди не галасли́ві?
lines.source: And the neighbors aren't noisy?
lines.source_literal: And neighbors not noisy?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Ні, буди́нок ти́хий. Па́ні, яка́ живе́ по́руч, працю́є в шко́лі, а над ва́ми живе́ стари́й лі́кар.
lines.source: No, the building is quiet. The lady who lives next door works at a school, and an old doctor lives above you.
lines.source_literal: No, building quiet. Lady, which lives nearby, works in school, and above you lives old doctor.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Скі́льки ко́штує кварти́ра на мі́сяць?
lines.source: How much is the apartment per month?
lines.source_literal: How-much costs apartment for month?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Два́дцять ти́сяч гри́вень.
lines.source: Twenty thousand hryvnias.
lines.source_literal: Twenty of-thousands of-hryvnias.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Чи мо́жна поба́чити кварти́ру за́втра?
lines.source: Could I see the apartment tomorrow?
lines.source_literal: Whether possible to-see apartment tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Так, прихо́дьте за́втра о шо́стій. Я бу́ду чека́ти бі́ля лі́фта.
lines.source: Yes, come tomorrow at six. I'll be waiting by the elevator.
lines.source_literal: Yes, come tomorrow at sixth. I will-be to-wait near elevator.

dialogues.title: Where does the sofa go?
dialogues.context: Oksana has just moved into a rented apartment, and Olena, Taras's sister, has come to help her decide where the furniture goes. They are friends and say 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Окса́но, яка́ світла́ віта́льня!
lines.source: Oksana, what a bright living room!
lines.source_literal: Oksana, what-kind bright living-room!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Дя́кую! Це кімна́та, яку́ я люблю́ найбі́льше.
lines.source: Thanks! It's the room I like best.
lines.source_literal: I-thank! This room, which I love most.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А де бу́де стоя́ти дива́н?
lines.source: And where will the sofa go?
lines.source_literal: And where will-be to-stand sofa?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Бі́ля вікна́, там, де за́раз лежа́ть мої́ кни́ги.
lines.source: By the window, where my books are lying now.
lines.source_literal: Near window, there, where now lie my books.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: До́бре. А ша́фа, яку́ тобі́ дала́ ма́ма?
lines.source: Fine. And the wardrobe your mom gave you?
lines.source_literal: Good. And wardrobe, which to-you gave mom?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Неха́й вона́ стої́ть бі́ля двере́й. Там бага́то мі́сця.
lines.source: Let it stand by the door. There's a lot of space there.
lines.source_literal: Let it stands near door. There much of-place.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А чия́ це гіта́ра, що лежи́ть на столі́?
lines.source: And whose guitar is that on the table?
lines.source_literal: And whose this guitar, that lies on table?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Тара́са. Він забу́в її́, коли́ допомага́в мені́ переї́хати.
lines.source: Taras's. He forgot it when he was helping me move.
lines.source_literal: Of-Taras. He forgot it, when helped to-me to-move.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А ще мені́ подо́бається те, що тут так ти́хо.
lines.source: And I also like how quiet it is here.
lines.source_literal: And also to-me pleases that, that here so quiet.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так. Вла́сник, у яко́го я оренду́ю кварти́ру, каза́в, що сусі́ди тут ти́хі.
lines.source: Yes. The landlord I rent the apartment from said the neighbors here are quiet.
lines.source_literal: Yes. Owner, at whom I rent apartment, said, that neighbors here quiet.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А лі́жко, яке́ стої́ть у спа́льні, нове́?
lines.source: And is the bed in the bedroom new?
lines.source_literal: And bed, which stands in bedroom, new?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Ні, старе́, але́ зру́чне. А тут бу́де стіл, за яки́м ми бу́демо обі́дати ра́зом.
lines.source: No, it's old, but comfortable. And here there will be a table where we'll have lunch together.
lines.source_literal: No, old, but comfortable. And here will-be table, at which we will-be to-have-lunch together.

dialogues.title: Should Sam take the apartment?
dialogues.context: The day after he saw the apartment, Sam tells his friend Taras about it. They say 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Се́ме, ти ба́чив кварти́ру, про яку́ ти мені́ каза́в?
lines.source: Sam, did you see the apartment you told me about?
lines.source_literal: Sam, you saw apartment, about which you to-me told?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, ба́чив. Вона́ світла́ й зру́чна, і там є балко́н, де мо́жна пи́ти ка́ву вра́нці.
lines.source: Yes, I did. It's bright and comfortable, and there's a balcony where you can drink coffee in the morning.
lines.source_literal: Yes, saw. It bright and comfortable, and there there-is balcony, where possible to-drink coffee in-the-morning.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А де той буди́нок?
lines.source: And where is the building?
lines.source_literal: And where that building?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Бі́ля па́рку, куди́ я ча́сто ходжу́ гуля́ти.
lines.source: Near the park where I often go for walks.
lines.source_literal: Near park, where-to I often go to-stroll.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А хто вла́сник?
lines.source: And who is the owner?
lines.source_literal: And who owner?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Його́ зва́ти Богда́н. Це чолові́к, чия́ ма́ма живе́ на пе́ршому по́версі.
lines.source: His name is Bohdan. He's a man whose mother lives on the first floor.
lines.source_literal: Him to-call Bohdan. This man, whose mom lives on first floor.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тоді́ вона́ зна́є всіх, хто там живе́.
lines.source: Then she knows everyone who lives there.
lines.source_literal: Then she knows all, who there lives.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так. Богда́н сказа́в, що той, хто живе́ в цьо́му буди́нку, ніко́ли не хо́че переї́хати.
lines.source: Yes. Bohdan said that whoever lives in this building never wants to move.
lines.source_literal: Yes. Bohdan said, that that, who lives in this building, never not wants to-move.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Мо́жливо, це пра́вда. А що тобі́ не подо́бається?
lines.source: Maybe that's true. And what don't you like?
lines.source_literal: Possibly, this truth. And what to-you not pleases?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Те, що буди́нок дале́ко від це́нтру.
lines.source: That the building is far from the center.
lines.source_literal: That, that building far from center.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А метро́ там є?
lines.source: Is there a metro there?
lines.source_literal: And metro there there-is?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, метро́ бли́зько.
lines.source: Yes, the metro is close.
lines.source_literal: Yes, metro close.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тоді́ бери́ її́ сього́дні, бо за́втра її́ мо́же взя́ти хтось і́нший.
lines.source: Then take it today, because tomorrow someone else may take it.
lines.source_literal: Then take it today, because tomorrow it can to-take someone other.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́бре, я подзвоню́ Богда́нові за́раз.
lines.source: OK, I'll phone Bohdan right now.
lines.source_literal: Good, I will-phone to-Bohdan now.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: две́рі, на по́версі, оголо́шення and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word in this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet and stress units, and each change in its forms is an alternation you have met before.

'Две́рі' [ˈdʋɛrʲi], door, is a plural-only noun, like 'гро́ші' and 'штани́': it has no singular form, so it names one door or several, and the words that agree with it are plural ('нові́ две́рі'). The 'в' before a vowel is [ʋ], as in 'вода́', and the 'р' is soft before 'і'. In the genitive the stress moves to the ending, which is '-ей', as in 'люде́й': 'бі́ля двере́й' [ˈbʲilʲɑ dʋɛˈrɛj], next to the door. 'Ме́блі', furniture, is plural-only too, and it keeps its stress: 'ме́блів'.

'По́верх', floor, takes '-і' in the locative. Masculine nouns whose stem ends in 'к', 'г' or 'х' take either '-у' ('у па́рку') or '-і', and the vocabulary note gives which. Before '-і' the 'х' becomes 'с', the same alternation that gives 'кни́га', 'у кни́зі': 'на по́версі' [nɑ ˈpɔʋɛrsʲi]. The new 'с' is soft because 'і' follows it. The other forms keep the 'х' ('по́верху'), and the singular keeps the stress on the first syllable.

'Оголо́шення' [ɔɦɔˈlɔʃɛnʲːɑ], advertisement, is built from the verb 'оголоси́ти', to announce, and two rules meet in it:

- Before the suffix '-ення' the 'с' of the verb becomes 'ш', as it does in 'писа́ти', 'пишу́'.
- The doubled 'нн' before 'я' is one long soft [nʲː], like the doubled consonant of 'життя́'.

The other new words follow rules you already know:

- In 'спа́льня' [ˈspɑlʲnʲɑ] and 'віта́льня' the soft sign makes the 'л' soft before 'н', as in 'ві́льний', and the 'н' is soft before 'я'.
- 'Буди́нок' has a fleeting 'о', like 'ри́нок': 'у буди́нку' [u buˈdɪnku].
- 'Ліфт' [lʲift] has one syllable and no stress mark; its genitive 'лі́фта' has two syllables and takes one. The 'л' is soft before 'і'.
- In 'зру́чний' [ˈzrut͡ʃnɪj] both 'ч' and 'н' are said, exactly as written.
- 'Лежа́ти' is a verb of the second conjugation, like 'сиді́ти'. Its stem ends in 'ж', which is always hard, so its endings are written with 'у' and 'а' where a soft consonant would take 'ю' and 'я': 'лежу́', 'лежи́ш', 'лежа́ть'.
- 'Орендува́ти' replaces '-ува-' by '-у-' in the present, like 'працюва́ти': 'оренду́ю', 'оренду́єш'.
- Every form of 'яки́й' is stressed on its ending: 'яко́го', 'яко́му', 'яку́', 'яки́ми'. The 'г' of '-ого' is the usual [ɦ].
- 'Під’ї́зд', the entrance of an apartment building in the culture note, has the apostrophe after the prefix 'під-', as 'в’ї́хати' has it after 'в-': it keeps the 'д' hard and shows that [j] is said separately: [pʲidˈjizd].
- In the second reading, 'тепло́', warmth, is the noun, and it differs from 'те́пло', it is warm, only by stress. 'Піч', stove, has 'і' in its closed syllable and 'е' when an ending opens the syllable: 'бі́ля пе́чі'. This is the alternation of 'стіл', 'на столі́', with 'е' in place of 'о'.

examples.target: Ша́фа стої́ть бі́ля двере́й.
examples.source: The wardrobe stands next to the door.

examples.target: Ми живемо́ на шо́стому по́версі.
examples.source: We live on the sixth floor.

examples.target: Окса́на чита́є оголо́шення.
examples.source: Oksana is reading the advertisements.

examples.target: Ключі́ лежа́ть на столі́.
examples.source: The keys are on the table.

examples.target: Спа́льня й віта́льня світлі́.
examples.source: The bedroom and the living room are bright.

grammar.title: Relative clauses with 'яки́й': gender and number from the noun, case from the clause
grammar.explanation:
A clause, as the unit on the future explained, is a part of a sentence with its own verb. A relative clause is a clause that describes a noun of the same sentence, the way 'that stands by the park' describes 'the building' in English. The noun it describes is its antecedent, because it comes before the clause. The word that opens the clause and points back to the antecedent is a relative pronoun. The main relative pronoun of Ukrainian is 'яки́й', the word you know from questions as 'what kind of?' and 'which?'.

A relative clause can be built from two sentences:

- 'Це буди́нок.', This is the building.
- 'Буди́нок стої́ть бі́ля па́рку.', The building stands by the park.

In the second sentence replace 'буди́нок' by 'яки́й', keep it at the front of its clause, and put the clause right after the noun: 'Це буди́нок, яки́й стої́ть бі́ля па́рку.', This is the building that stands by the park, literally 'this building, which stands near park'. English chooses among 'who', 'which' and 'that', and often leaves the word out, as in 'the apartment we rent'. Ukrainian never leaves it out, and one pronoun serves for people and for things: 'ді́вчина, яка́ тут живе́', the girl who lives here.

'Яки́й' has the endings of a hard adjective such as 'нови́й', and it takes its form from two places:

- its gender and number from the antecedent: 'буди́нок, яки́й', 'кварти́ра, яка́', 'лі́жко, яке́', 'сусі́ди, які́'
- its case from its own job inside the relative clause, the case the noun would have there

The gender and number are those of the antecedent as a word: 'ме́блі, які́' and 'две́рі, які́' are plural because these nouns are plural-only, and 'Мико́ла, яки́й' is masculine although the name ends in '-а'.

To find the case, say the clause as a sentence of its own, with the noun in place of the pronoun:

- 'кварти́ра, яка́ мені́ подо́бається': 'Кварти́ра мені́ подо́бається.' The apartment is the subject, so the pronoun is nominative: 'яка́'.
- 'кварти́ра, яку́ ми оренду́ємо': 'Ми оренду́ємо кварти́ру.' The apartment is the object, so the pronoun is accusative: 'яку́'.
- 'сусі́д, з яки́м я працю́ю': 'Я працю́ю з сусі́дом.' 'З' meaning 'with' takes the instrumental, so 'з яки́м'.
- 'буди́нок, у яко́му я живу́': 'Я живу́ в буди́нку.' The place is in the locative, so 'у яко́му'. After the comma, 'в' becomes 'у' before the [j] of 'яко́му', by the euphony rules.
- 'вла́сник, яко́му я дзвоню́': 'Я дзвоню́ вла́сникові.' 'Дзвони́ти' takes the person phoned in the dative, so 'яко́му'.
- 'мі́сто, до яко́го ми ї́демо': 'Ми ї́демо до мі́ста.' 'До' takes the genitive, so 'до яко́го'.

A preposition stands right before the pronoun, at the very start of the clause; English can leave it at the end ('the neighbor I work with'), and Ukrainian never does. The verb of the clause decides the preposition and the case, so learn them with the verb: 'жи́ти в' with the locative, 'говори́ти з' with the instrumental, 'ду́мати про' with the accusative. For a person or an animal the masculine and the plural accusative take the genitive form, as adjectives do: 'хло́пець, яко́го ти ба́чила', 'сусі́ди, яки́х ти ба́чила'. The feminine form 'яку́' does not change for people: 'ді́вчина, яку́ ти ба́чив'. When the subject of the clause is a noun, it often follows the verb: 'кварти́ра, яку́ оренду́є Тара́с', the apartment Taras rents.

A relative clause is always set off by commas: one before the clause, before the preposition if there is one, and one after it when the sentence goes on: 'Буди́нок, яки́й стої́ть бі́ля па́рку, нови́й.', The building that stands by the park is new. English puts commas only around a clause that adds something about a noun already identified ('my sister, who lives in Lviv') and none around a clause that says which one is meant ('the building that stands by the park'). Ukrainian writes the commas in both cases, so in Ukrainian the commas never show the difference; the context does.

'Котри́й', which you know from 'Котра́ годи́на?', can open a relative clause in the same way, with the same endings and the same meaning: 'буди́нок, котри́й стої́ть бі́ля па́рку', 'кварти́ра, котру́ ми оренду́ємо'. It is less common than 'яки́й' in modern standard Ukrainian. You will meet it in books, especially older ones, and in the speech of western Ukraine. Use 'яки́й' yourself, and recognize 'котри́й' when you read or hear it.

grammar.title: 'Що' as a relative word, 'той, хто' and 'те, що'
grammar.explanation:
'Що' can open a relative clause in place of 'яки́й': 'кни́га, що лежи́ть на столі́', the book that is lying on the table. As a relative word 'що' never changes: it shows no gender, number or case. Its most common use, and the only one this course asks of you, is where 'яки́й' would be in the nominative, as the subject of its clause, for people and for things alike: 'ді́вчина, що живе́ по́руч', the girl who lives next door. For every other job, and after any preposition, use 'яки́й', whose ending shows the case. 'Що' is common in speech, songs and stories; in writing 'яки́й' is the more usual choice.

Keep the relative word 'що' apart from the conjunction 'що', which joins a statement to a verb of saying or thinking, as in 'Я ду́маю, що він тут.', I think he is here. The conjunction stands for no noun and has no job in its clause. The relative word stands for its antecedent and is the subject of its clause, so you can replace it by 'яки́й': 'кни́га, яка́ лежи́ть на столі́'.

Sometimes a clause describes something the sentence does not name, as in English 'Whoever lives here knows the city' or 'I know what you are saying'. Ukrainian then supplies an antecedent, usually a form of the demonstrative 'той', and follows it with the question word 'хто' for people or 'що' for things, used as relative words:

- 'той, хто', the one who, whoever: 'Той, хто живе́ тут, зна́є це мі́сто.', literally 'that, who lives here, knows this city'
- 'те, що', what, that which: 'Я зна́ю те, що ти ка́жеш.', literally 'I know that, what you say'
- 'усі́, хто' or 'всі, хто', everyone who: 'Усі́, хто тут живе́, лю́блять цей парк.'

'Хто' usually takes a singular verb, even after 'усі́', while the verb of the main clause agrees with 'усі́' and is plural.

Each half of the pair takes its own case. 'Той' and 'те' take the case the main clause needs, with the forms of a demonstrative: 'того́' in the genitive, 'тому́' in the dative, 'тим' in the instrumental and 'на тому́' in the locative, while the accusative of 'те' is 'те'. 'Хто' and 'що' take the case their own clause needs, with the forms of the question words ('кого́', 'чого́'), unlike the relative word 'що' of the first paragraph, which never changes:

- 'Я ду́маю про те, що ти сказа́в.', I am thinking about what you said: 'те' is accusative after 'про', and 'що' is the object of 'сказа́в'.
- 'Я подзвони́в тому́, хто написа́в оголо́шення.', I phoned the person who wrote the advertisement: 'тому́' is the dative of 'той', because 'подзвони́ти' takes the dative, and 'хто' is the subject of 'написа́в'. The form 'тому́' here has the same spelling as the adverb 'тому́', therefore.

'Те, що' can also introduce a whole fact, and then the word 'що' in it is the conjunction described above: 'Мені́ подо́бається те, що тут ти́хо.', I like it that it is quiet here, literally 'to-me pleases that, that here quiet'. Here 'те' stands for the fact and is the subject of 'подо́бається'.

As in a relative clause, a comma separates 'той' or 'те' from 'хто' or 'що', and a second comma closes the clause when the sentence goes on.

grammar.title: Relative 'де', 'куди́', 'зві́дки', 'коли́' and 'чий'
grammar.explanation:
The question words for place can also open a relative clause after a noun that names a place, and they keep their question meanings:

- 'де', where something is or happens: 'мі́сто, де я живу́', the city where I live
- 'куди́', where to: 'парк, куди́ ми хо́димо гуля́ти', the park where we go for walks
- 'зві́дки', where from: 'мі́сто, зві́дки приї́хав Сем', the city Sam came from

'Де', 'куди́' and 'зві́дки' are adverbs, not pronouns: they stand for a place and never change. Together with the relative pronouns they are called relative words. Each of them can be replaced by 'яки́й' with a preposition, with the same meaning: 'мі́сто, у яко́му я живу́'; 'парк, до яко́го ми хо́димо'; 'мі́сто, з яко́го приї́хав Сем'.

English says 'where' for both 'де' and 'куди́', so choose by the verb of the clause, as in questions. A verb of being somewhere, such as 'жи́ти', 'працюва́ти' or 'стоя́ти', takes 'де'. A verb of going, such as 'іти́', 'ї́хати' or 'ходи́ти', takes 'куди́' when it means going to the place and 'зві́дки' when it means coming from it.

The antecedent can be the adverb 'там' or 'туди́' instead of a noun, which gives the English 'where' with no noun before it: 'Я живу́ там, де живе́ мій брат.', I live where my brother lives; 'Ми ї́демо туди́, куди́ ї́де Окса́на.', We are going where Oksana is going.

In the same way 'коли́' opens a relative clause after a noun of time: 'день, коли́ ми переї́хали', the day we moved.

'Чий', whose, opens a clause about an owner: 'сусі́дка, чий син гра́є на гіта́рі', the neighbor whose son plays the guitar. As in questions, 'чий' agrees with the thing owned, never with the owner, and the noun for the thing owned follows it at once:

- 'чий' before a masculine noun: 'сусі́дка, чий син гра́є на гіта́рі'
- 'чия́' before a feminine noun: 'чолові́к, чия́ ма́ма живе́ тут'
- 'чиє́' before a neuter noun: 'вла́сник, чиє́ оголо́шення я прочита́в'
- 'чиї́' before a plural: 'сусі́д, чиї́ ді́ти гра́ють у па́рку'

In everyday speech many people say 'у яко́го' or 'у яко́ї' instead, with the 'у' of 'у ме́не є': 'сусі́дка, у яко́ї син гра́є на гіта́рі', literally 'neighbor, at which son plays on guitar'. Both are correct.

culture.title: Apartments, rooms and floors
culture.text:
Most people in Ukrainian cities live in apartments. A typical city building has five, nine or more stories; many such buildings went up between the 1950s and the 1980s, and new ones, often much taller, are built in every large city. Ukrainians call a building of many stories 'багатоповерхі́вка', literally 'many-story-one', from 'бага́то' and 'по́верх'. Many families own the apartment they live in: after independence in 1991, residents could take ownership of the state apartments they lived in, and many did.

An apartment is named by the number of its rooms, and the kitchen, the bathroom and the hall are not counted. The three most common names are:

- 'однокімна́тна кварти́ра', a one-room apartment, where one room serves as living room and bedroom
- 'двокімна́тна кварти́ра', a two-room apartment, often a living room and a bedroom
- 'трикімна́тна кварти́ра', a three-room apartment

Each of these adjectives joins the first part of a numeral, 'одно-', 'дво-' or 'три-', to 'кімна́та'. In many older apartments the toilet is in a small room of its own, apart from the bathroom.

Floors are counted from the street: the floor at street level is 'пе́рший по́верх', as in American English, so 'на дру́гому по́версі' is one floor up. A large building has several entrances, each called 'під’ї́зд', with its own staircase and elevator, so a visitor needs the number of the building, of the entrance and of the apartment, and often a code for the door at the entrance.

People look for an apartment to rent through advertisements, most of them online, and through agents, who usually charge a fee. A tenant generally pays the first month's rent before moving in, and many landlords also ask for a deposit. The rent depends mostly on the part of the city, the number of rooms and the distance to the metro or to other transport.

paragraphs.target: Світла́ однокімна́тна кварти́ра на п’я́тому по́версі в буди́нку, яки́й стої́ть бі́ля метро́. У буди́нку є ліфт. Ку́хня вели́ка, а з кімна́ти мо́жна ви́йти на балко́н. Кварти́ра ко́штує ві́сім ти́сяч гри́вень на мі́сяць.
paragraphs.source: A bright one-room apartment on the fifth floor of a building that stands next to the metro. The building has an elevator. The kitchen is big, and you can step out of the room onto a balcony. The apartment costs eight thousand hryvnias a month.
paragraphs.source_literal: Bright one-room apartment on fifth floor in building, which stands near metro. In building there-is elevator. Kitchen big, and from room possible to-go-out onto balcony. Apartment costs eight of-thousands of-hryvnias for month.

paragraphs.target: Двокімна́тна кварти́ра для сім’ї́, яка́ хо́че жи́ти в ти́хому мі́сці. Віта́льня й спа́льня вели́кі й світлі́, а всі ме́блі нові́. По́руч парк і шко́ла, куди́ ді́ти мо́жуть ходи́ти самі́.
paragraphs.source: A two-room apartment for a family that wants to live in a quiet place. The living room and the bedroom are big and bright, and all the furniture is new. Nearby are a park and a school, where children can go on their own.
paragraphs.source_literal: Two-room apartment for family, which wants to-live in quiet place. Living-room and bedroom big and bright, and all furniture new. Nearby park and school, where-to children can to-go themselves.

paragraphs.target: Кімна́та для студе́нта або́ студе́нтки в кварти́рі, де вже живу́ть дві студе́нтки. Буди́нок стари́й, і лі́фта нема́є, але́ кімна́та зру́чна, а сусі́ди не галасли́ві.
paragraphs.source: A room for a male or female student in an apartment where two female students already live. The building is old and has no elevator, but the room is comfortable and the neighbors are not noisy.
paragraphs.source_literal: Room for male-student or female-student in apartment, where already live two female-students. Building old, and of-elevator there-is-not, but room comfortable, and neighbors not noisy.

paragraphs.target: Від буди́нку до університе́ту де́сять хвили́н. Кімна́та ко́штує чоти́ри ти́сячі гри́вень на мі́сяць. Той, хто хо́че поба́чити кімна́ту, мо́же подзвони́ти вла́сниці.
paragraphs.source: It is ten minutes from the building to the university. The room costs four thousand hryvnias a month. Anyone who wants to see the room can phone the owner.
paragraphs.source_literal: From building to university ten of-minutes. Room costs four thousands of-hryvnias for month. That, who wants to-see room, can to-phone to-owner.

paragraphs.target: Коли́сь украї́нська сім’я́ жила́ в ха́ті, яку́ вона́ сама́ будува́ла. Ха́та була́ невели́ка й бі́ла. У ній була́ кімна́та, де сім’я́ ї́ла, працюва́ла й спала́.
paragraphs.source: Long ago a Ukrainian family lived in a house that it built itself. The house was small and white. In it was a room where the family ate, worked and slept.
paragraphs.source_literal: Once Ukrainian family lived in house, which it itself built. House was not-big and white. In it was room, where family ate, worked and slept.

paragraphs.target: У ха́ті була́ вели́ка піч, яка́ дава́ла тепло́ всій сім’ї́. На ній ді́ти спа́ли взи́мку, коли́ було́ хо́лодно. А ще в ха́ті був стіл, за яки́м усі́ ра́зом обі́дали.
paragraphs.source: In the house there was a big stove that gave warmth to the whole family. The children slept on it in winter, when it was cold. The house also had a table at which everyone had lunch together.
paragraphs.source_literal: In house was big stove, which gave warmth to-whole family. On it children slept in-winter, when was cold. And also in house was table, at which all together had-lunch.

paragraphs.target: Сього́дні бага́то украї́нців живе́ в міста́х, у вели́ких буди́нках, де на ко́жному по́версі є кі́лька кварти́р.
paragraphs.source: Today many Ukrainians live in cities, in big buildings where every floor has several apartments.
paragraphs.source_literal: Today many of-Ukrainians lives in cities, in big buildings, where on each floor there-is several of-apartments.

paragraphs.target: У кварти́рі, де живе́ сім’я́, є ку́хня, де вона́ їсть, віта́льня, де вона́ відпочива́є, і спа́льня, де вона́ спить.
paragraphs.source: In the apartment where a family lives there is a kitchen, where it eats, a living room, where it rests, and a bedroom, where it sleeps.
paragraphs.source_literal: In apartment, where lives family, there-is kitchen, where it eats, living-room, where it rests, and bedroom, where it sleeps.

paragraphs.target: Але́ бага́то люде́й, які́ ви́росли в мі́сті, лю́блять ї́здити на вихідні́ в село́, де жили́ ї́хні бабу́сі й діду́сі. Там вони́ відпочива́ють від галасли́вого мі́ста.
paragraphs.source: But many people who grew up in the city like to go on weekends to the village where their grandmothers and grandfathers lived. There they rest from the noisy city.
paragraphs.source_literal: But many of-people, which grew-up in city, love to-go on weekend to village, where lived their grandmas and grandpas. There they rest from noisy city.

questions.prompt: In a traditional house, where did the children sleep in winter?
choices: On the stove
On a bed in the bedroom
On a table
questions.explanation: 'На ній ді́ти спа́ли взи́мку': 'ній' points back to 'піч', the stove that warmed the whole family.

questions.prompt: Where did everyone have lunch together?
choices: On the stove
In the bedroom
At a table
questions.explanation: 'А ще в ха́ті був стіл, за яки́м усі́ ра́зом обі́дали.' 'За яки́м' is 'at which', with 'яки́м' in the instrumental after 'за'.

questions.prompt: Why do many city people go to the village on weekends?
choices: To work in the old houses
To rest from the noisy city
To look for an apartment
questions.explanation: 'Там вони́ відпочива́ють від галасли́вого мі́ста.' They go to the village where their grandparents lived.

exercises.prompt: Match the rooms and furniture with their meanings
Match the Ukrainian words with their meanings

choices: The sofa stands next to the door.
The wardrobe stands next to the door.
The sofa stands next to the window.

exercises.prompt: Which verb says where a key or a book is when it is lying flat?
choices: стоя́ти
лежа́ти
сиді́ти
exercises.explanation: 'Лежа́ти' is for something lying flat: 'Ключ лежи́ть на столі́.' 'Стоя́ти' is for something upright, such as a wardrobe, and 'сиді́ти' is for a person or an animal sitting.

choices: A feminine noun in the singular
A neuter noun that never changes
A plural-only noun
exercises.explanation: 'Две́рі' has no singular form, like 'гро́ші': it names one door or several, and the words that agree with it are plural. So 'Ці две́рі нові́.' means 'This door is new.', with plural 'ці' and 'нові́'.

exercises.hint_source: I live on the third floor.
exercises.explanation: After 'на' the place is in the locative. 'По́верх' takes '-і', and the 'х' becomes 'с' before it: 'на по́версі'.

exercises.prompt: Why is it 'на по́версі', with 'с', when the noun is 'по́верх'?
choices: Before the ending '-і', 'х' becomes 'с', just as 'г' becomes 'з' in 'у кни́зі'.
The locative of every masculine noun ends in '-сі'.
The 'с' shows the stressed syllable.
exercises.explanation: Before '-і' the consonants 'к', 'г' and 'х' change to 'ц', 'з' and 'с'. The other forms keep the 'х': 'по́верху'.

exercises.prompt: The noun 'оголо́шення' is built from the verb 'оголоси́ти', to announce. Why does it have 'ш'?
choices: 'Ш' is the soft form of 'с' before every vowel.
Before the suffix '-ення' the 'с' of the verb becomes 'ш', as it does in 'писа́ти', 'пишу́'.
The noun comes from a different verb.
exercises.explanation: The alternation of 'с' and 'ш' is the one you know from 'писа́ти', 'пишу́'. The doubled 'нн' before 'я' is one long soft [nʲː], as in 'життя́'.

exercises.prompt: Why are the forms of 'лежа́ти' written 'лежу́' and 'лежа́ть', with 'у' and 'а'?
choices: The verb belongs to the first conjugation.
The stress is on the ending.
The stem ends in 'ж', which is always hard, so the endings are written with 'у' and 'а', not 'ю' and 'я'.
exercises.explanation: 'Лежа́ти' has the endings of the second conjugation, like 'сиді́ти'. After the hard 'ж' they are spelled 'лежу́', 'лежи́ш', 'лежа́ть'.

exercises.audio_target: Ді́вчина, яка́ живе́ над на́ми, ча́сто співа́є.
choices: The girl who lives next door often sings.
The girl who lives above us often sings.
The girl who lives above us often reads.

exercises.hint_source: This is the building that stands by the park.
exercises.explanation: The pronoun is masculine like 'буди́нок' and nominative because it is the subject of 'стої́ть': 'яки́й'. 'Що' also fits here, since it is the subject, and 'котри́й' is the less common equivalent.

exercises.prompt: Which form completes 'Ме́блі, ___ стоя́ть у віта́льні, нові́.'?
choices: яки́й
яке́
які́
exercises.explanation: 'Ме́блі' is a plural-only noun, so the pronoun is plural, 'які́', and so are 'стоя́ть' and 'нові́'.

exercises.hint_source: This is the apartment we rent. (a form of 'яки́й')
exercises.explanation: Feminine like 'кварти́ра', and accusative because it is the object of 'оренду́ємо': 'Ми оренду́ємо кварти́ру.'

exercises.prompt: In 'сусі́д, з яки́м я працю́ю', why is the pronoun 'яки́м'?
choices: It has the same case as 'сусі́д'.
'Яки́м' is the only form used after a comma.
It is masculine like 'сусі́д', and instrumental because 'з' in its own clause takes the instrumental.
exercises.explanation: Gender and number come from the antecedent, case from the clause: 'Я працю́ю з сусі́дом.' becomes 'з яки́м я працю́ю'.

exercises.prompt_target: Сусі́дка, з ___ я говори́в, живе́ на пе́ршому по́версі.
exercises.hint_source: The neighbor I talked to lives on the first floor. (a form of 'яки́й')
exercises.explanation: Feminine like 'сусі́дка', and instrumental after 'з': 'Я говори́в із сусі́дкою.' The feminine instrumental of 'яки́й' is 'яко́ю'.

exercises.hint_source: The building Olena lives in is old. (a form of 'яки́й')
exercises.explanation: Masculine like 'буди́нок', and locative after 'у' because it names the place: 'Оле́на живе́ в буди́нку.'

exercises.prompt_target: Сусі́да, ___ ти ба́чив учо́ра, зва́ти Богда́н.
exercises.hint_source: The neighbor you saw yesterday is called Bohdan. (a form of 'яки́й')
exercises.explanation: It is the object of 'ба́чив' and names a man, so the masculine accusative takes the genitive form, 'яко́го', as 'сусі́да' does.

exercises.prompt: Where does Ukrainian put commas around a relative clause?
choices: Only around a clause that adds something about a noun already identified
Before the clause, and after it when the sentence goes on, in every case
Only before the relative word, never after the clause
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian sets off every relative clause with commas, whether it tells which one is meant or only adds information: 'Буди́нок, яки́й стої́ть бі́ля па́рку, нови́й.'

exercises.audio_target: Той, хто живе́ тут, зна́є це мі́сто.
choices: Whoever works here knows this city.
Whoever lives here loves this city.
Whoever lives here knows this city.

exercises.prompt_target: Я ду́маю про ___, що ти сказа́в.
exercises.hint_source: I'm thinking about what you said.
exercises.explanation: 'Те, що' means 'what' with no noun before it. 'Те' takes the case of the main clause, the accusative after 'про', which for 'те' has the same form.

exercises.prompt: In 'Ключ, що лежи́ть на дива́ні, мій.', what is 'що'?
choices: The conjunction 'що', which joins a statement to a verb of saying or thinking
A relative word: it stands for 'ключ' and is the subject of 'лежи́ть'
The question word 'what?'
exercises.explanation: The clause describes 'ключ', and 'що' can be replaced by 'яки́й': 'Ключ, яки́й лежи́ть на дива́ні, мій.'

exercises.hint_source: This is the city where I grew up.
exercises.explanation: Growing up happens in a place, so the relative word is 'де', or 'у яко́му', with 'яки́й' in the locative.

exercises.hint_source: This is the park we go to for walks.
exercises.explanation: 'Ходи́ти' is a verb of going to the park, so the relative word is 'куди́', where to, not 'де'; 'до яко́го' and 'у яки́й' say the same with 'яки́й'.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Мі́сто, ___ приї́хав Сем, узи́мку ду́же холо́дне.'?
choices: де
куди́
зві́дки
exercises.explanation: Sam came from the city, so the clause needs 'зві́дки', where from. 'Куди́' is where to, and 'де' is where something is.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes 'Ді́вчина, ___ брат працю́є в ба́нку, живе́ по́руч.'?
choices: чий
чия́
чиї́
exercises.explanation: 'Чий' agrees with the thing owned, here 'брат', which is masculine, not with the owner, 'ді́вчина'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, who lives above the apartment?
choices: A lady who works at a school
An old doctor
Bohdan's mother
exercises.explanation: Bohdan says 'над ва́ми живе́ стари́й лі́кар'. The lady who works at a school lives next door.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, where will the wardrobe stand?
choices: By the window, where Oksana's books are lying
In the bedroom, next to the bed
By the door, where there is a lot of space
exercises.explanation: Oksana says 'Неха́й вона́ стої́ть бі́ля двере́й. Там бага́то мі́сця.' The sofa goes by the window.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, what does Sam not like about the apartment?
choices: The building is far from the center.
The neighbors are noisy.
There is no metro nearby.
exercises.explanation: Sam says 'Те, що буди́нок дале́ко від це́нтру.' The metro is close.

exercises.prompt_source: The apartment we rent is bright.
This is the city where I live.
This is the building where I live.
answers: Це буди́нок, у яко́му я живу́.
Це буди́нок, у котро́му я живу́.
exercises.explanation: Living is being in a place, so the relative word is 'де', or 'у яко́му', with 'яки́й' in the locative. A comma comes before the clause.

exercises.prompt_source: The sofa we bought is comfortable.
exercises.explanation: The pronoun is masculine like 'дива́н' and accusative as the object of 'купи́ли'. For a thing, the masculine accusative 'яки́й' has the same form as the nominative. Commas go before and after the relative clause.

answers: Той, хто живе́ тут, зна́є Богда́на.
Той, хто тут живе́, зна́є Богда́на.
Хто живе́ тут, той зна́є Богда́на.
Хто тут живе́, той зна́є Богда́на.
exercises.explanation: 'Whoever' is 'той, хто', with a comma between them and another after the clause. 'Богда́на' is the accusative of a man's name.

exercises.prompt_source: I know what you want. (to a friend)
answers: Я зна́ю те, що ти хо́чеш.
Я зна́ю те, чого́ ти хо́чеш.
exercises.explanation: 'What' with no noun before it is 'те, що', and 'те' may be left out after 'зна́ти'. 'Чого́', the genitive, is also natural after 'хоті́ти'.
